title: Dulce de leche, homemade
subtitle: Condensed milk caramelised to a thick, toffee-coloured spread
excerpt: Dulce de leche is a thick, sweet caramel made by slowly cooking sweetened condensed milk until it turns a deep golden brown and thickens to a spreadable paste. It takes about 2 hours by the tin-in-water method but produces a beautifully smooth result with no risk of burning.
sourceNotes: Dulce de leche (from Spanish: milk caramel) is a staple of South American confectionery, widely made at home by cooking sweetened condensed milk in its tin submerged in water. The method is well-documented across home cooking traditions from Argentina, Uruguay, and Brazil.

recipe.yieldDescription: 1 × 400 g tin of dulce de leche
recipe.freezeNotes: Keeps in the fridge for 3 weeks in a sealed jar. Freezes for 3 months.
recipe.batchNotes: Cook multiple tins in the same pan. Keep all tins submerged throughout.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Makes weeks ahead. Keeps refrigerated for 3 weeks.

glossaryTerms.definition: Literally 'sweet of milk' in Spanish. A thick golden-brown caramel paste made from sweetened condensed milk cooked for 2 or more hours. Used as a spread, cake filling, and ice cream sauce.

content.text: requires one tin of sweetened condensed milk and a large saucepan of water. The milk caramelises slowly inside its sealed tin as the water simmers around it. The result is smooth, thick, and deeply toffee-flavoured.
Remove the label from a 400 g tin of sweetened condensed milk. Do not open it.
Place the tin on its side in a deep saucepan. Cover completely with cold water by at least 5 cm. Bring to a gentle simmer.

Simmer for 2 hours for a pale, soft-set dulce de leche. Simmer for 2 hours 30 minutes for a darker, firmer spread. Top up with boiling water as needed to keep the tin covered at all times. The tin must never be allowed to boil dry.
Remove the tin with tongs and leave to cool completely before opening, at least 30 minutes. The contents are under pressure when hot; opening a hot tin is dangerous.

Spread directly from the tin onto toast or crackers. Swirl into ice cream, use as a layer cake filling, pipe into choux puffs, sandwich between biscuits, or drizzle over cheesecake. The flavour pairs particularly well with banana, chocolate, and toasted almonds.

attrs.title: Do not let the tin boil dry

content.text: A tin of condensed milk left without water in a hot pan can build pressure and rupture. Check the water level regularly throughout cooking and top up with boiling water to keep the tin fully submerged.
